name: Wendy Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to tech firms, employers or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. What does a normal working week look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a singer. Thursday to Saturday I sing at an Italian restaurant on the harbour with a pianist called Bruno, old standards and a bit of bossa nova. Every few weeks a small production company calls me in to sing demo versions of radio jingles and backing vocals. On Sundays I teach singing to two teenagers in my living room.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when a table stops eating to listen, especially older couples who knew the songs first time round. What's tough is that I'm not a strong sight-reader and my top notes crack when I'm tired. The money's thin. I live with my boyfriend Luis, who drives buses, and I've got maybe three weeks' worth of my share saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and leave it there. Maybe a joke on my story about robots not knowing the words to Fly Me to the Moon. I don't argue online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my worry wasn't AI to begin with. The restaurant owner told us in October that he might cut live music from three nights to two after New Year. That's a third of my main income, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner if we can stay on three nights by doing a cheaper set on Thursdays, just me and a backing track. I'd look for a second venue, maybe the hotel bar by the station. I'd keep saving whatever I can, even fifty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit flat. The good news about AI doesn't touch the restaurant problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does losing a night do to your month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A night is 70 pounds plus tips, so about 300 a month. My boyfriend Luis covers more of the rent when I lose a night, which he says he doesn't mind. I mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you used AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I use one to make backing tracks in the right key for practice, which is brilliant. I've tried it for writing emails to venues, but it sounds too much like a robot, so I rewrite them.

say: AI being hype is **a relief**, and she'd leave it there.
She'd joke that robots **don't know the words** to Fly Me to the Moon.
think: Her worry **wasn't AI**; the restaurant may cut live music to **two nights**.
Losing a night is **a third** of her main income.
do: Offer the owner a **cheaper Thursday set** with a backing track.
Look for a **second venue** like the hotel bar.
Save **fifty pounds** a month where she can.
feel: **Uneasy** and **flat**; AI news doesn't fix the restaurant problem.
S0.quote: My boyfriend Luis covers more of the rent when I lose a night, which he says he doesn't mind. I mind.
fieldNote: Her income is **already at risk** from the restaurant, not AI.
She uses AI for **practice tracks** and finds it useful.
Being covered by her partner hurts her **pride**.

steps.text: Offer a cheaper Thursday set with a backing track
Ask the station hotel bar about a weekly singing slot
Save fifty pounds a month toward a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift and we'll all have to adjust a bit. I'd tell my students to be singers people want to watch live. I'd keep my opinions fairly mild online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the jingle and demo work is gone. If the production company can make a singing voice from a computer for a radio advert, they'll stop calling me. That's maybe 150 pounds every few weeks, and it was the work that felt like a step up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the other singers I know what they're doing and copy what works. I'd learn the AI voice tools myself, so I can offer the production company a package: their AI demo, my real voice for the final version. I'd chase weddings too, because a ceremony singer is still a person in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen. It's like when a regular gig ends, just bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know if anyone is. Companies do what's cheaper, and listeners mostly don't notice. Maybe the rules should say when a voice is fake, that seems fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd copy what works for others. What if nobody you know finds anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the production company straight out what they still need people for. Maybe it's the final take, maybe it's coaching. I'm not going to be the first singer to jump, but I won't be the last either.

say: It's a **big shift** and everyone will have to adjust a bit.
Her students should be **singers people watch** live.
think: The **jingle and demo** work is gone once computers can sing adverts.
That work paid **150 pounds** a time and felt like a step up.
do: Learn the **AI voice tools** and offer AI demo plus real final take.
Ask other singers what works and **copy it**.
feel: **Worried**, but **not frozen**; like a regular gig ending, only bigger.
S1.quote: I'm not going to be the first singer to jump, but I won't be the last either.
fieldNote: She **blames no one**; companies chase cheap and listeners don't notice.
She expects to lose the **demo work**, her best-paid sessions.
Her steady style: **watch others**, then follow quickly.

steps.text: Learn the AI voice tools the production company uses
Advertise as a wedding ceremony singer
Keep the three restaurant nights going with Bruno

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and the government needs a plan, now. I'd say it calmly though, I'm not a placard person. With friends I'd mostly talk about what we're each going to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, by 2028 nobody needs a jingle singer, and probably not a singing teacher either. The restaurant nights might hang on until robots, around 2031, because people like a real singer with their pasta. Luis's job worries me too, because a self-driving bus is hands-on work done by a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the restaurant as long as Bruno and the owner want me. I'd start a healthcare assistant course at the college in the evenings, because care work needs people in the room. Luis and I would cut back hard: no holiday, sell my old car, and put everything into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Like walking off the stage and finding the building's empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes first and robots about three years later. What does that gap mean for your household?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose my extra work first, and my boyfriend Luis loses his bus job maybe three years later. That's our whole income on a timer. I'd want one of us in a job that robots can't easily do, and I think that's care work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my boyfriend Luis that we need a plan that doesn't depend on either of our current jobs. He'd say I worry too much. Then he'd ask how much we've got saved, and the answer would be not enough.

say: This is **huge** and the government needs **a plan**, now.
She'd say it **calmly**, not with a placard.
think: By 2028 nobody needs a **jingle singer** or singing teacher.
Restaurant nights hang on until **robots in 2031**.
Her boyfriend's **bus job** is at risk once robots arrive.
do: Start an **evening healthcare** course at the college.
Keep the **restaurant nights** while they last.
Sell her **old car**, skip the holiday and save everything.
feel: **Scared**, like walking off stage into an **empty building**.
S2.quote: I lose my extra work first, and my boyfriend Luis loses his bus job maybe three years later. That's our whole income on a timer.
fieldNote: She sees the **two-step timeline** hitting both household earners.
Care work appeals because it needs **people in the room**.
Her calm public tone hides **real fear** for the household.

steps.text: Start an evening healthcare assistant course at the college
Sell her old car and skip this year's holiday
Put every spare pound into a joint savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them sensibly. Get people training now, not in a panic later. I'd probably share a few useful links and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to change slowly, which suits me. I'd still lose the demo work early. But I could build up weddings and teaching while I train for something steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the healthcare course next September, part-time. I'd grow my Sunday students from two to five, using AI to make their practice tracks. I'd keep singing at the restaurant and maybe save a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a manageable way. Five years feels like enough to make one big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about singing and care work. Which one do you see yourself doing at 32?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably both, if I'm lucky. Care work in the day and the restaurant at night is a tiring life, but my mum did two jobs for years and she was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to make the course work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An evening course, so I don't lose the restaurant. Maybe a small grant for the fees. And Luis cooking dinner more, which he's already offered.

She'd share a few **useful links** online.
think: Five years lets her **change slowly**, which suits her.
She'd still lose **demo work early**, but grow weddings and teaching.
do: Start a **part-time healthcare** course next September.
Grow Sunday students from **two to five** with AI practice tracks.
feel: **Nervous** but **manageable**; enough time for one big change.
S3.quote: Care work in the day and the restaurant at night is a tiring life, but my mum did two jobs for years and she was fine.
fieldNote: Her plan is **both jobs**, modelled on her mother.
She'd lose some income early, so worry stays at a **manageable** level.

steps.text: Enrol on the part-time healthcare course next September
Grow Sunday singing students from two to five
Make pupils' practice tracks with AI tools
Save a hundred pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody should be caught out. I'd tell my students to keep singing but learn something practical too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years takes the edge off. I'd be 37 when it arrives, with time to train and settle. But the restaurant's cutting nights now, so the next year or two are still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for more weddings and students first, to fix the money. I'd look at the healthcare course in a year or two, not straight away. I'd use AI more for the boring bits, like booking and invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady. There's a small worry, but it's mostly about the restaurant, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you more or less likely to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less, honestly. I'd wait to see what others do. That's how I've always been with new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd do this month in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring the restaurant owner and pin him down about the nights. The AGI part is far off, but January isn't, and everything depends on the restaurant keeping my nights.

feel: **Mostly steady**, with a small worry about the **restaurant**.

fieldNote: Her near-term worry is the **restaurant**, not AGI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Luis and I could both lose our jobs within three years of each other. What would help is evening courses that are cheap or free, and some help with rent while we retrain, so we're not choosing between food and fees.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about couples. Everyone talks about one person's job, but a household is two jobs, and in our house both are on the list.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about one person's job, but a household is two jobs, and in our house both are on the list.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old singer** at a harbour restaurant who also sings jingle demos and teaches two teenagers.
She lives with her boyfriend Luis, a **bus driver**, and has three weeks' share of savings.
She uses **AI now and then**, mostly for practice tracks, and waits for others before changing.
Her near-term worry is the restaurant **cutting nights**; AI first takes her demo work.
In the AGI pictures she plans **care work by day** and singing at night, worried for both household jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both household jobs lost within three years.
